newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS/Spreads widen in some options.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS/Spreads widen in some options.

text.p: U.S. stock index options trading was fairly brisk Tuesday as the underlying markets rallied sharply, but some brokers said order flow was hampered by wide spreads.
"It's a quiet day for the most part," one broker in Chicago said. "It's hard to trade combos (combinations) and other things when people are quoting markets 3/4 to $1.
"So that slows us down," he said.
In the S&P 100 index .OEX, bid/ask spreads for February near the money options were generally 1/4 to 1/2 point, but widened out to 3/4 to one point in the March series.
Spreads in February S&P 500 index .SPX options were generally wider than in the February OEX options.
One trader said the wider spreads were mainly a function of the market's rally and strong demand.
By about 1315 CST/1915 GMT, the OEX was up nearly 11 points at 759.94, a gain of about 1.45 percent. The SPX was ahead 10.41 points, or about 1.35 percent, at 775.43.
Elsewhere the 30-stock Dow industrial average .DJI, was up 87 points at 6,748. It had reached a session high of 6,761.
Despite the rally, index put volume continued to largely outpace call volume.
At the CBOE, OEX put volume at 1300 CST/1900 GMT totaled 46,233 compared to call volume of 37,381. Put volume in the SPX was slightly lower than call volume, at 19,024 compared with 20,764 calls.
In the OEX, the busiest options included the February 700 and 705 puts and the February 760 and 770 calls.
Trading dropped off dramatically after the February series.
In the SPX, the February 800 call was by far the most active option, with 10,860 contracts changing hands.
The volume appeared to be new contracts as open interest in that contract was zero through Monday, when 11,481 contracts were closed.
The market's recovery was more than some analysts had been expecting, but its staying power depends in large part on whether bonds will be able to hold onto their own sharp gains.

"Put/call ratios were not exactly indicating a lot of fear with respect to this report," said Todd Salamone, senior analyst at Investment Research Institute, referring to the fourth quarter 1996 U.S. employment cost index report, which set bonds and stocks higher off the opening.
"The options activity on the index was not that indicative of a high level of fear, or the kind of extremes we look for," Salamone said.
He added that bonds' ability to maintain their gains would be a key to whether stocks can hold theirs.

In afternoon trading, U.S. debt futures cut some of their gains, with March Treasury bond futures slipping back below intraday support near 110-20/32, a level some technical analysts said the contract needed to close above to stay firm near term.
